facts.statement: VCS3 (nickname Putney) was introduced in 1969, designed by David Cockerell, as a portable synthesizer in a wooden cabinet whose modules are interconnected through a matrix patchboard.

Module complement: 3 VCOs, noise generator, 2 input amplifiers, ring modulator, voltage controlled low-pass filter, trapezoid envelope generator, voltage controlled reverberation, meter, 2 stereo output amplifiers, joystick.

VCS3 II (1973) added Prestopatch, changed the matrix layout and some circuitry, otherwise like the Mk I; 32x32 and 49x49 matrix boards (1974) link two VCS3 or Synthi A units via the Prestopatch sockets.
facts.locator: Sections 'Synthi VCS3 II', '32 x 32 Matrix', '49 x 49 Matrix'

facts.statement: DK1 (1969) is a velocity-sensitive monophonic keyboard for the VCS3 adding an extra VCO and VCA; DK2 (1972) is a duophonic version.
The current EMS home page says original-type Synthi A and VCS3 units are still in production, with spares and service for most original products; it lists Synthi A and VCS3 at GBP 5950 each.
facts.locator: Home page, top block and price list

facts.statement: The home page is stamped 'Last updated 5th May 2020', so whether prices and availability are current is not confirmed.
Patch pins are sold separately by the current maker at GBP 9.50 each.

After EMS (London) folded in 1979 its assets passed to Datanomics (small numbers of VCS3, Synthi AKS and Vocoders built 1980-84), then to composer Edward Williams; in April 1995 Robin Wood acquired the full EMS rights and Synthi A, VCS3 and vocoders continue to be built to original or modified specification.
EMS (London) Ltd. was formed in 1969 by Peter Zinovieff; the company collapsed in 1979 after heavy debt from the Hi-Fli guitar unit and other ventures.

Synthi 100 (1971, formerly Digitana, nickname Delaware) uses VCS3-type technology in a large console patched with two 60x60 matrix boards, one for signals and one for control voltages; fewer than 40 were built, mainly for universities and radio stations.

Module complement: 12 VCOs, 2 noise generators, 3 ring modulators, 4 low-pass and 4 high-pass VCFs, 3 trapezoid envelope generators, 2 reverbs, octave filter bank, slew limiter, envelope follower, pitch-to-voltage converter, 8 input and 8 stereo output amplifiers, 2 joysticks, 2 five-octave keyboards, 256-step digital sequencer, oscilloscope, frequency counter.
Introduced at GBP 6,500; the guide lists GBP 35,000 as its 1979 price.
Synthi A (1971, formerly Portabella) has the same specification and circuit boards as the VCS3 in an attache-case enclosure; Synthi AKS (1972) adds a KS sequencer and touch keyboard in the lid.

VCS3 and Synthi A are patched with pins in a matrix patchboard; the Synthi 100 uses two 60x60 boards (signal and control-voltage), and the 32x32 / 49x49 boards patch two instruments together through Prestopatch sockets.
Matrix patching was used on other EMS products, for example the Spectron video synthesizer with a 53x57 digital and a 16x20 analogue patch panel.
The VCS3 has three voltage-controlled oscillators (Synthi 100: twelve); waveform and frequency specifications are not given in the pages read.
The VCS3 has one voltage-controlled low-pass filter; the Synthi 100 has four low-pass plus four high-pass VCFs.
The VCS3 has one trapezoid envelope generator; the Synthi 100 has three. Shape and time specifications are not given in the pages read.
The VCS3 has a voltage controlled reverberation unit (Synthi 100: two); no specifications are given in the pages read.

Synthi Sequencer 256 (1971) stores 256 events of 42 bits (two 6-bit control voltages plus 13-bit start and stop times), runs from an internal 0.1-200 Hz clock or an external clock, and plays forwards or backwards; a 128-step version (also 32 and 64) existed.
KS sequencer (1972, as in Synthi AKS): 256 steps x 6-bit memory, sequence length 700 ms to 100 s, real-time and sequencer pitch outputs, transposition controls.

The product guide describes no electronic patch memory for the VCS3, Synthi A or Synthi 100: the patch is the set of pins in the matrix board. Digital storage is documented only for sequence data (Sequencer 256, KS). A DataSynthi with a programmable patch matrix was developed in 1980-84 but never produced.
facts.locator: Sections 'VCS3', 'Synthi 100', 'Synthi Sequencer 256' of the guide and 'The Inbetween Years' of the history

facts.statement: Sequencer 256 accepts an external clock; the Synthi 100 and Synthi A can be extended with keyboards and sequencers (DK1/DK2 for VCS3, KS in Synthi AKS). MIDI or computer interfaces are not mentioned in the pages read.
The VCS3 patch matrix is 16 x 16 (256 pin positions): rows are sources, columns are destinations, so a pin at one position joins one source to one destination.
The matrix is unbuffered, so adding a pin to a patch changes how other connections behave; patches are not exactly repeatable even with the same pin positions.
Pins contain resistors: white about 2.7 kohm (5% tolerance; measured spread 2,565-2,835 ohm), red 2.7 kohm with a tighter 2% tolerance, green higher resistance to attenuate a signal.

Wikipedia (Synthi A paragraph) gives 2.7 kohm pins with red = 1% and white = 5% tolerance, and green = 68 kohm attenuating pins. The red-pin tolerance (1% vs 2%) differs from the Sound On Sound figure.
The VCS3 Mk II (1973) added a Prestopatch socket accepting custom 16 x 16 plugs that mimic the matrix, giving a primitive way to recall a routing; knobs still had to be set by hand.
facts.locator: Part 2, paragraph on the VCS3 MkII

facts.statement: Wikipedia: VCS3 introduced by EMS in 1969; electronics largely by David Cockerell, appearance by Tristram Cary; about GBP 330 at launch; tuning instability from exponential conversion. It lists 3 oscillators (the third an LFO), noise, 2 input amplifiers, ring modulator, low-pass filter, trapezoid envelope generator, joystick, spring reverb and 2 output amplifiers.
Joystick range is only about +/-2 V, a voltmeter measures CVs or signals, and an oscilloscope output is on the rear panel. Stereo outputs A and B have independent level, pan and output filters.

Wikipedia: designed by David Cockerell and documented in 1971; GBP 6,500 originally; EMS built 30 units (the last one a Datanomics redesign sold to Cuenca, Spain). About six VCS3 worth of analogue modules; 12 VCOs and 8 VCFs; 85 circuit cards once the sequencer is included.
Two 60 x 60 pin matrices connect the modules, with an oscillator sync function from white pins (2.7 kohm).

Wikipedia describes the digital sequencer as three duophonic layers, 10,000 clock events and 256 duophonic note events; Sound On Sound calls it a six-track, 256-step sequencer. The descriptions differ in wording.

Sound On Sound: 12 VCOs, 2 noise generators, 3 ring modulators, 4 low-pass and 4 high-pass filters plus 39 other modules and an oscilloscope; two 5-octave velocity-sensitive keyboards; about 30 units built, almost all in universities or broadcasters, the BBC Radiophonic Workshop one being nicknamed The Delaware.
The two keyboards together give four control voltages and two key triggers; keyboard spread is adjustable, including microtonal tunings up to 61 divisions per semitone.

Wikipedia: Synthi A debuted May 1971, Synthi AKS March 1972 with built-in keyboard and sequencer; AKS retailed at about GBP 450; uses the VCS3 design in a briefcase with the same pin matrix. EMS (Robin Wood) still builds units.
The AKS sequencer is the KS (Keyboard Sequencer), a 256-event digital sequencer in the lid with a touch-sensitive Buchla-style keyboard.

Sound On Sound: the VCS3 follows neither 1 V/octave nor Hz/V. Internal scaling is 0.32 V/oct (oscillators 1 and 2), 0.26 V/oct (oscillator 3) and 0.20 V/oct (filter); because inputs have CV amplifiers, external CVs need about double: 0.64, 0.52 and 0.40 V/oct.
Signal levels are not the usual 10 V peak-to-peak: oscillator outputs are 3, 4 or 6 V depending on waveform, the filter 5 V and the noise generator 3 V (per Sound On Sound).

The WebSearch summary of bigbluewave.co.uk also gives sub-1V/oct scalings (0.32/0.26/0.20 V/oct internal), giving similar numbers; the pages themselves were not read, so it is not independent confirmation.
Four 1/4-inch rear inputs (two microphone, two line) feed the Channel 1 and 2 rows of the matrix; the DK1 keyboard cable carries two power rails, two CVs and a gate for the envelope shaper.

Oscillators 1 and 2 cover below 1 Hz to about 10 kHz. Osc 1 outputs sine and sawtooth (with rectifying shape), osc 2 pulse and triangle with waveshapers, and osc 3 pulse and triangle in a low range of 0.025 Hz to about 500 Hz. On an unmodified unit the waveshapers are not voltage controlled.

The WebSearch summary of another spec page gives oscillator ranges of 0.5 Hz-20 kHz and 1 Hz-10 kHz / 1 Hz-100 kHz for osc 1/2, which disagree with each other; text unread. Both are kept as unreliable.

Sound On Sound says the low-pass filter is often described as 18 dB/octave but has a knee: 12 dB/octave in the first octave above cutoff, then 18 dB/octave. High resonance (EMS: response) lowers low-frequency gain, so EMS called it low-pass/band-pass, and it self-oscillates.
Wikipedia states 24 dB/octave for the VCS3 filter, with a citation-needed tag. This conflicts with the 12/18 dB figure.

The envelope generator (Shaper) has six controls: Attack about 2 ms-1 s; On (hold) claimed 0-2.5 s; Decay claimed 3 ms-15 s; Off (delay before auto retrigger) set to 10/Manual for normal playing; separate Trapezoid and Signal levels; a manual Attack button. It can auto-repeat up to 60 Hz.
The author measured a hold of about 5 s and decay of about 60 s on his unit, longer than EMS claimed (3 ms-15 s decay).

The DK1 keyboard connects through a dedicated 8-way cable (two power rails, two CVs, gate). Channel switches select Signal/CV1 and Dynamic Voltage/CV2; the DK1 has its own sawtooth oscillator and VCA with a spread control. Keyboard CVs enter via two input-level controls, so 1:1 tracking needs tuning.
EMS sold a special jack lead to allow conventional MIDI/CV operation, and the rear panel has an oscilloscope output.
Two Matrix products linked Prestopatch sockets of two Synthi A or VCS3 Mk II instruments (with or without keyboard sockets).
To recreate a patch one must record knob positions, the matrix pin map, and which pin (by resistance) sits in each position because pins vary.
DK1 (1969) is an early velocity-sensitive monophonic keyboard with an extra VCO and VCA; DK2 (1972) is duophonic.
Outputs A and B drive the left/right speakers with level, pan and bass/treble filters; the X/Y joystick has about +/-2 V range; a voltmeter and a rear oscilloscope output allow patch checking.
Computer Synthi added a PDP-8 minicomputer with 4 Kb RAM, an LED display, twin digital cassettes and two 24 x 60 matrix patchboards; only three were sold.
The Vocoder 5000 has a 22-band filter, mic/line inputs, 22 x 22 matrix patchboard, two oscillators and noise, a frequency shifter, pitch-to-voltage extractor and a spectrum display driver.
